title: People v. Shaw
description: Whether a gun discovered in an apartment should be suppressed because the defendant's arrest was a "constructive entry" in violation of Payton v New York and the tenant's subsequent consent to search was involuntary or not sufficiently attenuated from the illegal arrest.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued there was no Payton violation as the defendant was arrested outside the apartment and lacked standing to challenge the search, and that the tenant's consent was voluntary and attenuated from any illegality.
defendant_argument: Samuel Shaw argued the gun should be suppressed because his arrest violated Payton due to coercive police tactics constituting a "constructive entry," and the tenant's consent to search was involuntary and not sufficiently attenuated from this illegal arrest.
decision_outcome: The court modified the Appellate Division's order, affirming that the defendant's arrest violated Payton, but remitted the case to the Appellate Division to apply the correct legal standard for determining the voluntariness of the tenant's consent to search, specifically for the charge of criminal possession of a weapon in the second degree (count nine).

title: Clarke v. Town of Newburgh
description: Whether the Town and Town Board of Newburgh, as subordinate governmental entities, can maintain a facial constitutional challenge to the vote dilution provision of the New York Voting Rights Act.
plaintiff_argument: The respondents (Oral Clarke, et al.) argued that Newburgh, as a political subdivision, lacks the capacity to challenge the constitutionality of a state law like the NYVRA, based on long-standing New York legal precedent.
defendant_argument: The appellants (Town of Newburgh, et al.) argued that they can bring a facial constitutional challenge to the NYVRA's vote-dilution provision, claiming that compliance with the statute would force them to violate constitutional equal protection clauses, fitting a narrow 'dilemma' exception.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, holding that Newburgh, as a political subdivision, cannot assert a facial constitutional challenge to the NYVRA's vote-dilution provision because it failed to demonstrate that compliance would force it to violate equal protection.

title: People v. Sargeant
description: Whether a defendant may forfeit the constitutional right to a trial by a jury of 12 persons by engaging in egregious misconduct, with the plaintiff arguing that such misconduct leads to forfeiture and the defendant arguing against it, seeking a mistrial.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the defendant forfeited his right to a trial by a jury of 12 due to his egregious misconduct of intentionally tampering with a deliberating juror, which necessitated the juror's discharge and left no alternate jurors.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that he did not waive his right to a 12-person jury and that continuing with 11 jurors would be inappropriate, contending that a single instance of misconduct should not result in the forfeiture of this right.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, holding that the trial court properly exercised its discretion in proceeding with the remaining 11 jurors after the defendant forfeited his right to a 12-person jury through egregious misconduct.

title: Onondaga v. New York
description: Whether the Even Year Election Law (EYEL) is an unconstitutional exercise of legislative authority that violates the home rule provisions of Article IX of the State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the EYEL violates Article IX of the State Constitution by infringing on counties' constitutional right to set the timing of county elections and terms of office, and that the EYEL is neither a general nor a duly enacted special law.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the EYEL is constitutional because it is a general law that does not violate Article IX of the State Constitution, and it serves the legitimate state interest of increasing voter turnout and reducing confusion by consolidating local elections with state and federal elections.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that the Even Year Election Law is constitutional and does not violate the New York Constitution.

title: Glen Oaks Village Owners v. City of New York
description: Whether New York City's Local Law No. 97, which aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from large buildings, is preempted by the State's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, with plaintiffs arguing for preemption and defendants arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that Local Law No. 97 is preempted by the Climate Act because the State has occupied the field of regulating greenhouse gas emissions, implying a need for statewide uniformity.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the Climate Act does not preempt Local Law No. 97, as the State Legislature did not express or imply an intent to occupy the entire field and explicitly encouraged complementary local action.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, granting the defendants' motion and holding that the Climate Act does not preempt New York City's Local Law No. 97.

title: Cuomo v. New York State Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government
description: Whether the Ethics Commission Reform Act of 2022 unconstitutionally vests the State Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government with executive power, thereby violating the separation of powers doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Act is unconstitutional because it empowers the Commission to exercise executive powers without sufficient gubernatorial accountability, specifically regarding the appointment and removal of commissioners.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that New York's constitution permits the Legislature to vest executive power with politically independent bodies to enforce ethics and lobbying laws against executive officials, requiring such autonomy.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the Ethics Commission Reform Act of 2022 is not unconstitutional on its face and does not violate the separation of powers doctrine.

title: Amedure v. State
description: Whether Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) violates the equal representation mandate in article II, section 8 of the New York Constitution and principles of judicial review.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) violates the equal representation mandate by allowing a ballot to be processed as valid even with a split board decision, and improperly restricts judicial review, potentially enabling electoral fraud.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) is constitutional, secures equal representation, and does not unconstitutionally constrain the judiciary, as sufficient safeguards against fraud exist.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) does not violate the constitutional principles of equal representation, separation of powers, or judicial review.

title: Fossella v. Adams
description: Whether Local Law 11, which allows noncitizens to vote in municipal elections, violates the New York State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the New York State Constitution's Article II, Section 1 limits voting exclusively to citizens, making Local Law 11 unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Article II, Section 1 merely sets a minimum standard for citizen voting and does not prohibit localities from expanding the franchise to noncitizens under their home rule authority.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Local Law 11 is unconstitutional because the New York State Constitution limits voting to citizens, affirming the injunction against its implementation.

title: Stefanik v. Hochul
description: Whether New York's Early Mail Voter Act, which permits all registered voters to vote early by mail, is constitutional under Article II, Section 2 of the New York Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Early Mail Voter Act is unconstitutional because Article II, Section 2 of the New York Constitution historically mandates in-person voting, and the retention of specific absentee voting provisions implies a prohibition on universal mail-in voting, a stance reinforced by voters rejecting a constitutional amendment to allow no-excuse absentee voting.
defendant_argument: The Early Mail Voter Act is constitutional because the New York Constitution does not explicitly prohibit mail-in voting, especially after the 1966 amendment removed the in-person voting requirement, and Article II, Section 7 grants the legislature broad power to determine election methods.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that New York's Early Mail Voter Act is constitutional and does not violate the New York Constitution.

title: People v. Watkins
description: Whether trial counsel was constitutionally ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification instruction at the close of the trial.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that trial counsel was not ineffective because, at the time of the trial, a cross-racial identification instruction was discretionary, not mandatory, and therefore, the failure to request it did not constitute ineffective assistance of counsel.
defendant_argument: Mark Watkins argued that his trial counsel was ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification instruction, especially given the cross-racial nature of the identification and its importance.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the order of the Appellate Division, ruling that trial counsel was not constitutionally ineffective.

title: People v. Debellis
description: Whether Anthony Debellis received ineffective assistance of counsel because his attorney failed to request a jury instruction on the statutory defense of voluntary surrender for criminal possession of a weapon, instead pursuing a meritless common-law defense.
plaintiff_argument: Counsel was not ineffective because the defendant was not entitled to a voluntary surrender instruction, and counsel's overall performance was not deficient.
defendant_argument: Counsel was ineffective for failing to request the voluntary surrender defense instruction, which was supported by trial testimony, and instead pursuing an inapplicable temporary and lawful possession defense, thereby depriving him of a fair trial.
decision_outcome: The order of the Appellate Division is reversed, and a new trial is ordered for Anthony Debellis.

title: People v. Rodriguez
description: Whether police interference with a bicyclist constitutes a seizure requiring reasonable suspicion of a criminal offense or probable cause of a Vehicle and Traffic Law violation, with the plaintiff arguing it does not and the defendant arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the police stop of the defendant on his bicycle was not a seizure or was justified by founded suspicion, and thus did not violate his constitutional rights.
defendant_argument: Lance Rodriguez argued that the police stop of his bicycle was an unlawful seizure without reasonable suspicion or probable cause, violating his federal and state constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, granted the defendant's motion to suppress the gun and statements, and dismissed the indictment.

title: Hoffmann v. New York State Independent Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) has a continuing constitutional duty to prepare and submit new legislative redistricting plans for future elections, or if the court-drawn maps from the 2022 election are the exclusive and decade-long remedy.
plaintiff_argument: The IRC has a continuing constitutional duty to prepare and submit a second redistricting plan, even though the 2022 congressional map was judicially adopted, because the court-drawn maps were only an interim remedy for the 2022 election.
defendant_argument: The IRC's deadline to submit a second redistricting plan passed on February 28, 2022, making any current attempt to compel them unconstitutional and untimely, and the court-ordered redistricting plan from Harkenrider is the exclusive remedy that should remain in effect until the 2030 census.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, compelling the Independent Redistricting Commission to reconvene and submit a second redistricting plan and implementing legislation by February 28, 2024.

title: Police Benevolent Association v. City of New York
description: Whether section 10-181 of the Administrative Code of the City of New York, which criminalizes the use of certain restraints by police officers during an arrest, violates the New York Constitution on either preemption or due process grounds.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the local law is unconstitutional because it is preempted by state laws governing police arrest authority and is void for vagueness, particularly regarding the compression of an arrestee's diaphragm, failing to provide adequate notice of prohibited conduct.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the local law is a proper exercise of its home rule authority, is not preempted by state law, and is not vague because police officers receive training on the prohibited conduct.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Administrative Code § 10-181 is constitutional and is neither preempted by state law nor void for vagueness.

title: Stevens v. New York State Division of Criminal Justice Services
description: Whether the legislature's grant of rulemaking authority to the Commission on Forensic Sciences was sufficient to authorize the Commission's promulgation of the Familial DNA Search Regulations.
plaintiff_argument: The Commission lacked statutory authority to promulgate the Familial DNA Search Regulations, violating the separation of powers doctrine, and the policy is arbitrary and capricious, disproportionately affecting African-Americans and innocent people.
defendant_argument: The Commission had the statutory authority to promulgate the Familial DNA Search Regulations, and the petitioners lacked standing to challenge them.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division's order, holding that the Commission had the statutory authority to promulgate the Familial DNA Search Regulations and dismissing the petition.

title: People v. Regan
description: Whether the defendant's constitutional right to a prompt prosecution was violated by an excessive pre-indictment delay of over four years, warranting the dismissal of the indictment.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the delay, though lengthy, did not violate the defendant's due process rights, citing the seriousness of the charge and the absence of demonstrated prejudice to the defendant.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the excessive and largely unexplained pre-indictment delay of over four years violated his constitutional right to a prompt prosecution, regardless of whether he could prove specific prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order and dismissed the indictment, finding that the excessive and unexplained pre-indictment delay violated the defendant's constitutional right to a prompt prosecution.

title: Owner Operator Independent Drivers Association v. NYS Department of Transportation
description: Whether New York regulations requiring electronic logging devices (ELDs) in commercial motor vehicles and authorizing warrantless inspections of ELD data violate the State Constitution's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that New York's ELD rule, which mandates warrantless inspections of ELD data, constitutes an unreasonable search and seizure under the State Constitution and fails to adequately limit the frequency of such searches.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the ELD rule's warrantless inspections fall under the administrative search exception to the warrant requirement for pervasively regulated industries and are constitutional under the State Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the New York regulations adopting the ELD rule, which authorizes warrantless inspections, are facially constitutional and do not violate the State Constitution's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.

title: St. Lawrence Cnty. v. City of Ogdensburg
description: Whether Local Law No. 2-2021 of the City of Ogdensburg, which repealed a prior local law opting out of Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) article 11, is inconsistent with RPTL 1150 or unconstitutional under the home rule article of the New York State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, St. Lawrence County, argued that Local Law No. 2 is inconsistent with RPTL 1150 because it circumvents the need for an agreement and unconstitutionally impairs the County's powers by shifting financial liability for delinquent taxes without an agreement.
defendant_argument: The defendant, City of Ogdensburg, argued that Local Law No. 2 is a valid exercise of its power to opt back into RPTL article 11, and that RPTL 1102 (6)(b) allows the County to become responsible for tax enforcement without a specific agreement, thus not violating state law or impairing the County's powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Local Law No. 2-2021 of the City of Ogdensburg is valid and enforceable.

title: People v. Johnson
description: Whether the police had reasonable suspicion to justify a level three stop and frisk of Tyquan Johnson under the De Bour framework, with the plaintiff arguing that the police action was justified and the defendant arguing it was not.
plaintiff_argument: The police action, including the stop and frisk, was justified at its inception and at every subsequent stage of the encounter leading to Mr. Johnson's arrest, based on his movements and appearance.
defendant_argument: The police lacked the requisite level of suspicion to justify an intrusion under any level of the De Bour framework, specifically that his actions did not constitute reasonable suspicion for a level three stop and frisk.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the police lacked reasonable suspicion for the stop and frisk, and dismissed the indictment against Tyquan Johnson.

title: Delgado v. State
description: Whether the enabling act that tasked a Committee with determining salary increases for legislators and state officials constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the enabling act unconstitutionally delegated legislative authority to the Committee and violated the constitutional requirement that legislative salaries be "fixed by law."
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the enabling act is constitutional as it is a valid assignment of power to a temporary commission with a discrete purpose and set standards, and the Legislature retained authority to modify or reject recommendations.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the enabling act has not been shown to be unconstitutional.

title: Harkenrider v. Hochul
description: Whether the legislature's 2022 congressional and state senate redistricting maps are unconstitutional due to procedural failures by the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) and the legislature, and due to unconstitutional partisan gerrymandering.
plaintiff_argument: The legislature's redistricting maps were unconstitutionally enacted because the IRC failed to submit a second redistricting plan as required, and the congressional map was unconstitutionally gerrymandered to favor the majority party.
defendant_argument: Petitioners lacked standing, the IRC's failure did not strip the legislature of its authority to enact redistricting plans, and petitioners failed to prove the maps were unconstitutionally partisan.
decision_outcome: The court declared the congressional and state senate maps void due to procedural unconstitutionality and substantive partisan gerrymandering, and remitted the case to the Supreme Court for new maps to be drawn with the assistance of a special master.

title: People v. Dawson
description: Whether Malik Dawson unequivocally invoked his right to counsel during police interrogation, with the plaintiff arguing his request was equivocal and the defendant arguing it was unequivocal.
plaintiff_argument: The defendant's inquiries and demeanor suggested only a conditional interest in speaking with an attorney, and he did not unequivocally invoke his right to counsel, thus his waiver of Miranda rights was valid.
defendant_argument: Malik Dawson unequivocally and repeatedly asked to contact his lawyer, and therefore his subsequent waiver of Miranda rights without counsel present was invalid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, upholding the conviction and the finding that the defendant did not unequivocally invoke his right to counsel.

title: White v. Cuomo
description: Whether Article 14 of the Racing, Pari-Mutuel Wagering and Breeding Law, which authorizes interactive fantasy sports contests, violates the New York Constitution's prohibition on gambling.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that interactive fantasy sports contests constitute unlawful gambling because their outcomes depend to a material degree on chance, as participants cannot control the performance of real-life athletes.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that interactive fantasy sports contests are skill-based competitions, not gambling, because contestants use significant skill and knowledge to select their rosters, which substantially influences the outcome.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Article 14 of the Racing, Pari-Mutuel Wagering and Breeding Law does not violate the New York Constitution's prohibition on gambling.

title: People v. Torres
description: Whether the Right of Way Law, which imposes criminal liability based on ordinary negligence for drivers who injure pedestrians or bicyclists, violates due process or is preempted by state law.
plaintiff_argument: The People of the State of New York argued that the Right of Way Law is constitutional and not preempted by state law, asserting that ordinary negligence is a sufficient mens rea for criminal liability and that the law does not conflict with or is preempted by the Penal Law or Vehicle and Traffic Law.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Right of Way Law is unconstitutional, violating due process by employing an 'ordinary care' mens rea for criminal liability, and that it is preempted by state law, specifically the Penal Law and Vehicle and Traffic Law.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Term's orders in both cases, rejecting the defendants' constitutional and preemption challenges to the Right of Way Law.

title: People v. Schneider
description: Whether a Kings County Supreme Court Justice had jurisdiction to issue eavesdropping warrants for defendant's cell phones, which were not physically present in New York, for the purpose of gathering evidence in an investigation of enterprise corruption and gambling offenses committed in Kings County.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that eavesdropping warrants are executed in the geographical jurisdiction where law enforcement officers intentionally intercept communications, regardless of the physical location of the target or device.
defendant_argument: Schneider argued that the Kings County Supreme Court Justice lacked jurisdiction because his cell phones and call participants were not physically present in New York, meaning the warrants were not 'executed' in Kings County.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the Kings County Supreme Court Justice had jurisdiction to issue the eavesdropping warrants.

title: Protect the Adirondacks! Inc. v. New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
description: Whether the state's plan to construct approximately 27 miles of Class II community connector trails for snowmobile use in the Forest Preserve is permissible under the New York Constitution's "forever wild" provision, which prohibits the destruction of timber and mandates the preservation of wild forest lands.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the construction of the Class II trails, requiring the cutting and destruction of substantial timber and creating an artificial man-made setting, violates the "forever wild" provision of the New York Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the destruction of trees is not significant, and the project's impacts are justified as it enhances public access to the Preserve and provides various recreational opportunities, consistent with the "forever wild" provision's intent for public use.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, holding that the planned construction of the Class II community connector trails would violate the "forever wild" provision of the New York State Constitution.

title: People v. Gordon
description: Whether a search warrant authorizing the search of "entire premises" implicitly permits the search of vehicles located on those premises, even if the vehicles are not specifically mentioned in the warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that a warrant to search an "entire premises" may impliedly authorize a search of automobiles found on the property, relying on federal caselaw that treats vehicles as containers.
defendant_argument: Mr. Gordon argued that police lacked particularized probable cause to search the vehicles because the warrant did not specifically mention them, nor did the warrant application provide probable cause for searching the vehicles.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' decision to suppress the physical evidence seized from the two vehicles, ruling that the search warrant did not authorize the search of the vehicles.
